p.src: After Qin Zhong died, Baoyu wept inconsolably. Only after Li Gui and the others had spent half the day coaxing and comforting him did he finally stop, and even on his return he remained desolate and grief-stricken. Grandmother Jia contributed several dozen taels of silver and separately prepared funeral offerings, while Baoyu went to burn paper money in mourning. Seven days later, the coffin was borne away and buried; there is nothing further to relate. Baoyu alone thought of him and mourned him every day, though there was nothing he could do. After an unknown length of time, Jia Zhen and the others came one day to report to Jia Zheng: “All the work in the garden has now been completed. The Elder Master has inspected it, and we are only waiting for you to look it over. If anything is amiss, it can be altered before the tablets and couplets are inscribed.” Jia Zheng pondered for a while, then said, “Those tablets and couplets present a real difficulty. Properly speaking, we ought to ask the Imperial Consort to bestow the inscriptions. Yet unless she sees the scenery herself, she will most likely be unwilling to compose them rashly. On the other hand, if we wait until after Her Highness’s visit to request them, such extensive grounds and so many pavilions will look bleak and uninteresting without names or inscriptions; even flowers, willows, hills, and streams could never display their full charm.” The literary retainers standing nearby replied with smiles, “Your venerable judgment is entirely correct. We have a humble suggestion: the tablets and couplets must by no means be omitted, but neither should their names be made final. For the present, we might compose provisional phrases of two, three, or four characters to suit the character of each scene, make them into illuminated tablets and couplets, and hang them up temporarily. Then, when the Imperial Consort comes to visit, we can ask her to settle the names. Would that not satisfy both needs?” Jia Zheng and the others heard this and all said, “That is a sound proposal. Let us go and look around today and freely suggest inscriptions. If they prove suitable, we shall use them; if not, we can invite Yucun to compose new ones.” The others laughed. “Whatever you compose today, sir, is certain to be excellent. Why wait for Yucun?” Jia Zheng smiled. “You do not understand. Even in my youth I was only mediocre at composing inscriptions on flowers, birds, hills, and streams. Now that I am older and burdened with official paperwork, I have grown still less practiced in such writings as soothe the heart and delight the senses. Even if I devise something, it will inevitably be pedantic and stiff, and instead of enhancing the flowers, willows, gardens, and pavilions, it will fail to harmonize with them and prove utterly pointless.” The literary retainers laughed. “That need cause no concern. Once we have all seen the place, each of us can submit his best proposal; we shall retain the good and discard the poor. There is no reason why that should not do.” Jia Zheng said, “That is perfectly sound. Fortunately, the weather is mild and warm today. Let us all go for a stroll.” With that, he rose and led the company on their way.

p.src: Jia Zhen went ahead to notify everyone in the garden. As it happened, Baoyu had lately been sunk in unrelieved sorrow over Qin Zhong, so Grandmother Jia often had attendants take him into the garden to amuse himself. He had only just entered it now when Jia Zhen suddenly approached and said to him with a smile, “Why have you not gone out yet? Your father will be here at any moment.” At this, Baoyu gathered his wet nurse and pages and dashed out of the garden like a puff of smoke. He had just rounded a bend when he came face-to-face with Jia Zheng leading the guests toward him. Unable to hide in time, he could only stand to one side. Jia Zheng had recently heard the schoolmaster praise Baoyu’s particular skill in matching couplets, saying that although the boy disliked study, he seemed to possess a certain wayward talent. p.src: Just as Jia Zheng reached the garden gate, Jia Zhen appeared with a large number of stewards and attendants, who stood waiting respectfully to one side. Jia Zheng said, “Have all the garden gates closed. We shall inspect the outside before going in.” On hearing this, Jia Zhen ordered the gates shut. Jia Zheng first stood squarely before the main gate to inspect it. The main entrance consisted of five bays, roofed with rounded tiles and loach-back ridges. The door frames and latticed windows were all finely carved in fresh designs, without any red paint or colored ornament. The surrounding walls were uniformly finished in smoothly polished plaster, while the white stone terrace below was carved with patterns of exotic western foliage. Looking to either side, he saw snow-white plaster walls with irregular courses of tiger-skin stone laid along their bases to follow the terrain. The design had indeed avoided the vulgar conventions of ostentatious splendor, and he was naturally pleased. He then ordered the gates opened, whereupon a range of green crags appeared directly ahead, blocking the view. All the literary retainers exclaimed, “What a splendid hill! What a splendid hill!” Jia Zheng said, “Without this hill, every prospect in the garden would meet the eye the moment one entered. What pleasure would there be in that?” The others said, “Precisely. Only one who bears great hills and valleys within his breast could ever have conceived of this.” When they had finished speaking, they looked ahead and saw rugged white rocks rising steeply, some shaped like demons and others like savage beasts, rearing in every direction. Their surfaces were mottled with moss and half-veiled by trailing vines, amid which a narrow, twisting path could just be glimpsed. Jia Zheng said, “Let us follow this little path on our tour, and return by way of the other side. Then we shall be able to see everything.”

p.src: Having said this, he ordered Jia Zhen to lead the way; then, supporting Baoyu by the arm, he followed the winding path into the opening among the rocks. Looking up, he suddenly saw a smooth, mirror-like slab of white stone on the hill, clearly intended to bear an inscription facing the entrance. Jia Zheng turned and asked with a smile, “Gentlemen, what name do you think would suit this place best?” At this, some proposed the two characters “Layered Green,” others “Brocade Crags,” still others “Rival to Incense-Burner Peak” or “Little Zhongnan”; dozens of different names were suggested. In fact, the guests had long understood that Jia Zheng meant to test Baoyu’s progress and attainments, so they merely put forward a few conventional phrases to fill the occasion. Baoyu too had guessed his father’s intention. After listening to them, Jia Zheng turned and ordered Baoyu to propose a name. Baoyu said, “I once heard an ancient saying: ‘To compile anew is not so good as to transmit the old; carving in the antique manner is ultimately finer than sculpting in the modern style.’ Moreover, this is not the principal hill or the garden’s main prospect, so there is really nothing here that calls for a special name; it is merely the first step toward discovering the scenery beyond. It would be better simply to inscribe the old poetic line, ‘A winding path leads to a secluded place.’ That would have both dignity and breadth.” On hearing this, everyone praised him: “Exactly so! Young Master Bao, your natural gifts are lofty and your literary imagination far-reaching, quite unlike those of us whose minds have gone stale from too much book-learning.” Jia Zheng smiled. “Do not praise him absurdly. He is young and merely makes one scrap of knowledge serve ten purposes; it is only good for a laugh. We shall consider other proposals later.”

Everyone exclaimed, “What a delightful place!” They all went in and found, immediately beyond the entrance, a winding covered walkway, while the path below the steps was paved with pebbles. Beyond it stood two or three small rooms, one bright central chamber flanked by two inner ones. Inside, the beds, side tables, chairs, and desks had all been built to fit the available space. A small door in an inner room led out into the rear courtyard, where a large pear tree grew beside plantains. There were also two small rear rooms. At the foot of the rear wall, an opening had been made to admit a stream. A channel scarcely a foot wide carried it inside the wall; it wound around the steps and along the house into the front courtyard, then circled beneath the bamboo and flowed out again.

p.src: Presently Jia Lian hurried over, and Jia Zheng asked him how many varieties there were in all, how many had arrived, and how many were still lacking. At this question Jia Lian hastily drew from the leg of his boot a folded paper tucked inside it. After glancing through the abbreviated list, he replied, “There are one hundred and twenty sets of large and small hangings in various silks and gauzes, including embroidered python designs, raised embroidery, kesi tapestry, and ink-patterned fabrics. Eighty sets arrived yesterday, leaving forty still to come. All two hundred curtains arrived yesterday. Besides these, there are two hundred scarlet felt curtains, two hundred red-lacquered bamboo blinds woven with golden-thread vine, two hundred black-lacquered bamboo blinds, and two hundred multicolored cordwork curtains with coiled-flower patterns. Half of each kind has arrived, and all should be complete by autumn. The chair covers, table valances, bed valances, and table covers—twelve hundred of each set—have arrived as well.” They talked as they walked, when suddenly a green hill slanted across their path. Rounding into the embrace of the hill, they saw dimly revealed a stretch of low wall built of yellow earth, its top thatched with rice stalks. Several hundred apricot trees stood there in bloom, like leaping flames amid billowing rosy clouds. Within stood several bays of thatched cottages. Outside grew mulberries, elms, hibiscus, cudrania, and other trees, whose tender new shoots had been woven along their natural bends into two rows of green hedges. Beyond the hedge, below the hillside, was an earthen well, with a sweep, windlass, and similar apparatus beside it. Below, plots and furrows stretched out in rows, and fine vegetables and flowering greens spread as far as the eye could see.

Suddenly they heard the murmur of water spilling from a rocky cavern; creepers hung down above it, while fallen blossoms drifted below. “What a beautiful scene! What a beautiful scene!” they all exclaimed. “What name would you gentlemen give it?” asked Jia Zheng. “There is no need to devise another,” they replied. “The three characters ‘Wuling Spring’ fit it perfectly.” Jia Zheng laughed. “Again, too literal—and stale besides.” The others laughed. “Then the four characters ‘The Qin People’s Ancient Dwelling’ would do as well.” “That is even more explicit,” said Baoyu. “‘The Qin People’s Ancient Dwelling’ alludes to fleeing from disorder. As they were about to enter the inlet cavern, they suddenly wondered whether a boat was available. “There are four lotus-gathering boats and one pleasure boat,” said Jia Zhen, “but they have not yet been completed.” Jia Zheng laughed. “What a pity we cannot enter.” “We can also enter by the winding mountain path,” said Jia Zhen. Suddenly, beneath the willow shade, a zigzag plank bridge with vermilion railings came into view. Crossing it, they found paths leading in every direction and saw a cool, airy lodge with uniformly polished brick walls, dark tiles, and ornamental openwork masonry. p.src: “This house is exceedingly dull,” remarked Jia Zheng. But as he stepped through the gate, an immense, intricately formed rock suddenly towered before him, piercing the sky. Rocks of every shape clustered around it on all sides, completely concealing every building within, and there was not a single flowering plant or tree. Instead, they saw a profusion of strange herbs: some trailed tendrils, some sent out runners, some hung from the peaks, and others thrust through cracks in the rocks; some even drooped from the eaves, twined round pillars, fringed the masonry, or coiled over the steps. Some fluttered like green ribbons, some curled like golden cords; some bore fruit red as cinnabar, others flowers like golden osmanthus. Their rich fragrance was unlike any ordinary floral scent. Jia Zheng could not help laughing. “How intriguing! “But I recognize hardly any of them.” Someone suggested, “They are fig creepers and wisteria.” “Fig creepers and wisteria could never have such an extraordinary fragrance,” said Jia Zheng. “Indeed, they are not,” said Baoyu. “Though some fig creepers and wisteria are mixed among them. “The fragrant ones are sweetflag and hengwu; that kind is probably angelica, this one kudzu, that one golden-parasol grass, and this one jade-dew vine. That may well be what happened here.” Before he could finish, Jia Zheng shouted, “Who asked you?” Baoyu recoiled in fright and dared say no more.

p.src: With that, they all came out. They had not gone far when they beheld a magnificent pavilion rising loftily before them, with tier upon tier of upper stories. Exquisite halls embraced it on every side, while elevated passageways wound away into the distance; green pines brushed the eaves, jade balustrades encircled the terraces, gilded beast masks gleamed, and brightly painted dragon heads shone. Jia Zheng said, “This is the main hall, then. It is merely a little too sumptuous.” They all replied, “Only such splendor is fitting. Although the Imperial Consort esteems frugality, naturally detests excess, and delights in simplicity, her present exalted rank demands such ceremony. This is by no means excessive.” As they talked and walked, a white-jade ceremonial archway appeared directly ahead, exquisitely carved with coiling dragons and guardian chi-dragons. Jia Zheng asked, “What inscription should be placed here?” The others replied, “‘The Immortal Realm of Penglai’ would surely be best.” Jia Zheng shook his head without a word. At the sight of this place, something suddenly stirred in Baoyu’s heart. It seemed to him that he had seen it somewhere before, yet he could not recall when or under what circumstances. Jia Zheng again ordered him to devise an inscription, but Baoyu was wholly absorbed in pondering the scene before him and had no thought for the task. Not knowing what was in his mind, the others assumed that the torment of the past half-day had exhausted his spirits and drained his talent and words. If they continued to test and press him, he might grow desperate and cause some mishap, which would be awkward. They therefore hastened to urge Jia Zheng, “Enough, enough. Let him compose it tomorrow.” Jia Zheng himself feared that the Lady Dowager might become anxious, so he sneered, “Even a wretch like you has moments when he is unable to perform, it seems. Just then, a servant came to report that someone sent by Yucun had arrived with a message. Jia Zheng smiled. “We shall not be able to visit the remaining places. Even so, we must eventually leave by the other side. Though we cannot inspect them closely, we may at least take a brief look.” With that, he led his guests onward. When they reached a great bridge, they saw water rushing in like a crystal curtain. The bridge was in fact built over the sluice connecting with the river outside, through which the spring water was drawn into the garden. Jia Zheng therefore asked, “What is this sluice called?” Baoyu replied, “This is the very source of the Fragrant Spring, so it should be called the ‘Fragrance-Diffusing Sluice.’” “Nonsense,” said Jia Zheng. “I expressly refuse to use the words ‘Diffusing Fragrance.’” As they continued on their way, they passed serene halls and thatched cottages, walls piled from stones, and windows woven from flowering branches; beneath a hill stood a secluded Buddhist nunnery, while amid the woods lay hidden the alchemical chamber of Daoist women. There were long galleries and winding grottoes, square halls and round pavilions, but Jia Zheng had no time to enter any of them. He remarked that his legs ached after half a day without rest. Just then another courtyard appeared ahead, and Jia Zheng laughed. “Now that we are here, we must go in and rest awhile.” So saying, he led them straight around the flowering peach trees and through a moon gate woven from a screen of bamboo and blossoms. In a moment they saw whitewashed walls enclosing the place and green willows drooping all around. Jia Zheng and the others went inside. As soon as they passed through the gate, they found covered galleries joined together on both sides. Several rocks adorned the courtyard. On one side grew several clumps of plantain; on the other stood a Xifu crabapple, spreading like a parasol, its fine green sprays hanging like silken threads and its blossoms opening as red as cinnabar. p.src: As he spoke, he led them into the rooms. They saw that these rooms were arranged quite differently from the others, so that it was impossible to tell where one ended and another began. On every side were exquisitely pierced wooden panels, carved with designs such as “Clouds and a Hundred Bats,” “The Three Friends of Winter,” landscapes and figures, birds and flowers, assorted treasures, ancient curios, or myriad variations on the characters for good fortune and longevity; all were the work of master craftsmen, painted in five colors, picked out in gold, and inlaid with precious stones. The panels formed compartment after compartment: some held books, some displayed tripods, some accommodated brushes and inkstones, while others were fitted for flowers and vases or for miniature landscapes. These compartments came in every conceivable shape: round above and square below, like sunflower blossoms or plantain leaves, or like linked rings and half jade discs. It was truly a profusion of splendor, intricate and exquisitely translucent. Here, a sudden stretch of five-colored gauze proved to cover a tiny window; there, a light veil of colored damask turned out to conceal a secluded door. Moreover, the walls were covered with recesses cut precisely to the shapes of the antiques and curios they contained. Thus zithers, swords, hanging vases, table screens, and the like, though mounted on the walls, lay perfectly flush with their surfaces. Everyone praised it: “What an exquisitely ingenious design! How could anyone ever have conceived it?” By now Jia Zheng and the others had entered, but before they had passed through even two sections, they had already lost the way by which they had come. To the left there seemed to be a door they could pass through, and to the right a window appeared to divide the space; yet when they approached, a bookcase blocked their way. When they turned back, they again saw bright gauze windows and what looked like a passable doorway. But on reaching it, they suddenly found another party coming toward them, every person identical in appearance to themselves—it was their reflection in a huge glass mirror. Once they passed around the mirror, even more doors appeared. Jia Zhen laughed. “Sir, follow me. This door leads to the rear courtyard, and going out through there is actually a shorter way than the one we took before.” As he spoke, he led them around two more layers of gauze screens and brocade panels. Sure enough, they found a door and went out. The courtyard was filled with trellises of roses and roses of Sharon. After passing the floral screen, they found a clear stream barring their way. Everyone exclaimed in surprise, “Where does this stream come from?” Pointing into the distance, Jia Zhen said, “It begins at that sluice and flows to the mouth of that cave. From there it is channeled through the northeastern mountain hollow to the village, while another branch is cut toward the southwest. In the end, all the streams reach this spot, join together again, and flow out beneath that wall.” On hearing this, everyone said, “Marvelous indeed!” As they spoke, a great mountain suddenly blocked their path. “We have lost our way,” they all said. Jia Zhen laughed. “Follow me.” He resumed his place at their head, and they followed him until, with a sudden turn around the foot of the mountain, they came upon a broad, level avenue and saw the great gate open out clearly before them. Everyone cried, “Delightful, delightful! It is the very height of inspired ingenuity!” Thereupon they all went out. Baoyu, however, remained wholly preoccupied with all he had seen inside. Since Jia Zheng had given him no order to leave, he had no choice but to follow the party to the study.
